1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4.background: Named after Szymon Winawer and pioneered by Aron Nimzowitsch and Mikhail Botvinnik. Thanks in great part to Botvinnik in the 1940s it became the most often seen reply to 3.Nc3, until 3...Nf6 revived in the 1980s and overtook it in popularity.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5.strategy: Pushes past the pin: with the c3 knight tied down, e4 cannot be defended by a recapture, so the pawn advances and gains space, supported by d4. The centre closes, White has more room on the kingside, and Black attacks the base of the chain.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine-Maróczy Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2.strategy: A gambit: the knight develops and leaves e4 to be taken. If Black accepts, a quick a3 puts the question to the bishop, and when it takes on c3 the knight recaptures, so White keeps a healthy pawn structure and a lead in development, but must show compensation for the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Delayed Exchange Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5.strategy: Resolves the tension by trading pawns, which frees Black's c8 bishop. With Nc3 and ...Bb4 added to the exchange structure, White can provoke ...Bxc3 with a3 and get an asymmetrical pawn structure, so the game is less drawish than the plain exchange.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, the natural reflex, and keeps the tension. But it blocks the queen's support of d4 and creates no real problems: Black can take on e4 or strike at d4 and reach equality without difficulty.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once. After ...Bxc3+ bxc3 White has the bishop pair and a half-open b-file, and Black's kingside lacks its dark-squared bishop, but the doubled pawns are a lasting liability and e4 needs looking after.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.background: Frank Marshall first played it, against Mikhail Chigorin in 1901; Rashid Nezhmetdinov also played it, notably against Mikhail Tal. The name is said to come from a game between Alexander Alekhine and Salomon Flohr, in which Alekhine wanted to play the Bogoljubow Variation but mixed up his move order and played 4.Bd2 instead of 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.strategy: Breaks the pin and offers the e4 pawn for quick development and pressure on g7, where the f8-bishop no longer stands guard. Black can take the pawn and the game stays roughly level, but White must keep playing actively; sound, though sharper and riskier than the main moves.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+.strategy: Takes the knight before it can be chased, doubling White's pawns on the c-file at the cost of the dark-squared bishop. That bishop is Black's good piece and its absence leaves the dark squares near the king, g7 above all, short of cover, but the damaged pawn structure is a lasting trump.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Ba5.strategy: Avoids the exchange, but the bishop is chased again by the b-pawn, which gains queenside space with tempo. Black has spent several moves on the bishop while White's centre stays untouched, and the cramped French set-up gets worse.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Be7.strategy: Retreats and gives up the pin, so White's a3 was a free tempo. Black keeps the bishop and avoids doubled pawns, but is left in a cramped position with nothing to show for ...Bb4, while White gains space at once.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.strategy: The natural recapture: it gives White doubled c-pawns, but also a strong centre, a half-open b-file and the bishop pair against a kingside without its dark-squared bishop. White has attacking chances if the position stays open; in a closed game the pawn structure favours Black.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.B.strategy: Avoids doubled pawns, but the bishop defends neither d4 nor b2: Black takes the d4 pawn with the bishop, or the b2 pawn, and is a clean pawn up.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.Q.strategy: Hangs the queen: the bishop on c3 takes it with check, and the bishop that recaptures is a poor return for the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.strategy: Takes the pawn that the last move left without a defender and opens the centre. Black is a pawn up for the moment, but must watch the dark squares around g7, where White's queen can strike.

Attacks the base of White's centre at once and keeps the pawn on d5. If White pushes e5, the familiar main-line structure arises with the bishop already traded; White can also release the tension, but the centre then comes under fire.

Develops the knight, which also guards d5, and prepares to castle. Without the bishop the g7 pawn is loose, so Qg4 is an immediate shot that Black has to meet carefully, and the move does not strike at the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Winckelmann-Reimer Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn from the side and offers a second pawn as a gambit: if Black takes, White recaptures with a lead in development. Black does better to strike back in the centre at once.

The queen attacks g7 and the e4 pawn in one move: with Black's dark-squared bishop gone, g7 has no defender. Black has to give something back, so the extra pawn is in doubt, and White's bishop pair and half-open b-file add to the pressure.

Attacks the e4 pawn quietly and keeps the queen safe in the centre. Black defends the pawn without trouble, so White gets back nothing at once, but the bishop pair and the centre give some compensation for the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: White broke the pin without defending e4, so Black wins a pawn and opens the centre. White now has to prove that quick development and play against g7 are worth the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops, supporting the d5 pawn and keeping the structure intact. It is safe, but it hands White time to untangle, where taking the pawn makes White prove the compensation.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Bxc3.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight, but the d2 bishop recaptures and White's pawns stay healthy, so the usual trump of the exchange is missing. Black can still take on e4 afterwards, but concedes the bishop pair and has made little of the pin.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.strategy: The point of the gambit: the queen attacks g7, which has lost its bishop's protection, and the e4 pawn at once. Black cannot keep everything, but White's queen comes out early and has to justify the pawn with threats.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once, but the d2 bishop blocks the queen's protection of d4: Black takes it with the queen, regains a pawn and attacks the knight on e4 as well.

Develops and defends d4, so the queen cannot grab a second pawn. But it does nothing about the lost e4 pawn: Black keeps it and develops, and White has no attack yet to show for it. Playable, but less active than going for g7.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.strategy: Attacks the queen and defends e4 in one move, so Black keeps the extra pawn for now. The price is g7: if the queen takes it, Black gets time to harass the queen and the material stays level.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation, Kunin Double Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.background: Most opening databases call it the Kunin double gambit. The earliest game found with a player named Kunin is Vladimir Kunin against Oschengoit, 1958, which became a popular miniature. The line was known before: it had already appeared at the 1950 Candidates in a game between Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.strategy: Takes a second pawn and covers g7 with the queen in the same move. The exposed queen invites trouble, though: after castling long the rook stands behind the d2-bishop and each bishop move uncovers an attack on it. The position stays balanced, but it is sharper and riskier than the main line.
Shuts the queen out of g7 with a pawn, but gives the e4 pawn straight back: Qxe4 regains the material. The dark squares around f6 and h6 are left weaker, with no bishop to guard them.

Takes the pawn and attacks the h8 rook in the same move. The queen is far from the rest of White's pieces, though, and Black's reply gains time to harass it, so White has to watch Black's lead in development.
Steps out of the attack while keeping the g-file and pressure on g7. Black keeps the extra pawn and can develop in peace, so White's compensation rests on the lead in development alone.
Takes the pawn but walks into ...Nxe4: the knight on f6 guards e4, and the queen is lost for a knight.
Saves the rook with tempo by attacking the queen, and the rook takes the open g-file, pointing at g2. Black has traded the g7 pawn for activity and development.
Saves the rook by retreating it, covering f7, but gives up the g-file and the pressure on g2. White can take on h7 as well, and Black has nothing to show for the second pawn.
Grabs a pawn but leaves the h8 rook hanging: Qxh8+ wins a whole rook for the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.Nb.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation, Schwarz's Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.Nb.strategy: A sharp idea: the knight steps back so that the d2 bishop attacks the undefended bishop on b4 and asks for a trade. It costs two knight moves and leaves e4 hanging, so Black can take the pawn after the exchange while White is behind in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.e5.strategy: Gains space and fixes the pawn chain, the standard White set-up against this pin. The bishop on d2 already guards c3, so a trade on c3 can be recaptured without doubling the pawns; Black has to work against the base of the chain.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.ex.strategy: Releases the tension and heads for a symmetrical, open-centred game with the pinned knight on c3. It is safe and level, but White gives up the grip on e5 and cannot expect more than equality.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Strikes at the base of the white centre at once: with the bishop on d3 blocking the queen, d4 is attacked and has no defender, while the knight on c3 is pinned. White has to deal with the pawn before anything else.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once. The bishop has to recapture and spend a second move there, so Black reaches an easy, equal game: the knight comes out, Black castles and has a central pawn break ready.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 Ne7.strategy: Develops the knight, guards d5 and prepares to castle. It is a sound set-up, but it does not use the loose d4 pawn, and White gets time to organise the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.strategy: Opens the centre by trading pawns instead of defending d4. The c3 knight is pinned, so it cannot retake on d5, and White relies on getting the pin undone with tempo; meanwhile d4 stays under fire.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.dxc.strategy: Resolves the tension by capturing, so the loose d4 pawn is no longer a target and the pinned knight is left alone. The pawn will not last, but Black spends time winning it back while White finishes development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.Ne2.strategy: Defends d4 and the c3 knight, but shuts the bishop in: after ...c4 the bishop on d3 is attacked and has no square, since the knight on e2 and the pawns on c2 and e4 block it. White gives up the bishop for a pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.strategy: Recaptures with the queen in the centre, where it hits both d4 and g2, and the pinned knight cannot challenge it. Black gets an active queen early, which White must try to hunt by unpinning.

Recaptures with the pawn, the solid way: the queen stays at home and the d5 pawn holds the centre. A check on the open e-file only forces a reply, and the c5 pawn still presses on d4, so the game stays balanced.
Takes the knight and doubles White's pawns after bxc3, but gives up the pin and hands White the bishop pair and an open centre. The d5 pawn can then be won back with the queen.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Kondratiyev Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.strategy: Breaks the pin by putting the bishop behind the knight, so that the knight now attacks the queen on d5. White offers the loose d4 and g2 pawns for tempo and development: a risky exchange of pawns for activity.

Removes the weak d4 pawn by capturing and wins a pawn for the moment. Black cannot recapture with the bishop, since ...Bxc5 allows Nxd5, and a queen recapture leaves the c3 knight pinned and under fire, so White must finish development with care.
Attacks the queen but hangs the bishop: the knight on c3 is pinned and cannot recapture, so ...Qxe4+ simply wins a piece.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping a solid, symmetrical centre and the pin on c3. With the knight on c3 and the bishop on b4 inserted, the game is less drawish than the plain Exchange: White can try to show that the bishop is misplaced, usually by provoking the exchange on c3 with a3.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen instead of the pawn, leaving the e6 pawn at home and unbalancing the symmetrical structure. The queen takes the centre at once and eyes d4 and the long diagonal toward g2, but it comes out early, and the bishop on c8 stays shut in behind e6.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 Bxc3+.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once, so White gets the doubled c-pawns and the bishop pair without spending a tempo on a3. A sound simplification, but Black hands over the pin for nothing and plays without its more active bishop.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..strategy: Develops the bishop on its natural diagonal, where it bears on h7 and prepares castling. White keeps the symmetrical structure; the usual way to unbalance it is a3, provoking the exchange on c3 and leaving an asymmetrical pawn structure after bxc3.

Puts the question to the bishop at once. If it takes on c3, White gets the bishop pair and an asymmetrical pawn structure instead of the drawish mirror image; if it retreats, Black has lost time. The cost is that White's kingside pieces are still at home.

Gives check and offers to trade queens. If the queens come off, the position is symmetrical and harmless, and White has given up the chance to show that the bishop on b4 is misplaced. Sound, but it takes the tension out of the game.

Develops the knight to a square from which it guards d5 and can reach f5 to block the bishop's diagonal or g6 to challenge a queen on h5. The cost is that h7 is guarded only by the rook, which invites a queen sortie, so Black must be alert on that diagonal.

Develops the queen's knight with an attack on d4 and keeps e7 free for the king's knight. Black accepts the usual plan of a3 and an exchange on c3, which leaves an asymmetrical structure that is balanced. Simple, healthy development is all this position asks of Black.
Develops the king's knight to its natural square, covering d5 and e4. It runs into the bishop sortie to g5, which pins the knight to the queen and costs Black time to untangle.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Exchange Variation, Canal Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..strategy: Brings the queen out so that it and the bishop on d3 both bear on h7, which only the rook guards, and Black has to meet the threat at once. But the queen is exposed early and can be driven off with gain of time, so the attack achieves little against accurate defence.

Puts the question to the bishop, the plan this line is built around: after ...Bxc3+ bxc3 White has the bishop pair and a solid pawn centre for the doubled c-pawns, in an asymmetrical position far less drawish than the plain Exchange. If the bishop retreats, Black has lost time.

Develops the knight to a square where it guards both c3 and d4, so the pin loses its sting and an exchange on c3 can be met by recapturing with the knight, without doubled pawns. White gets a harmonious set-up and an early castle, but the structure stays symmetrical and the game calm.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: the pawn on e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and cannot be defended by the pinned knight on c3, so Black wins it. White must now show that its lead in development is worth the pawn, and Black has to meet that with care.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6.strategy: Declines the offered pawn and develops, adding a second attacker on e4, which the pinned knight on c3 cannot defend. It sidesteps the gambit but passes up the extra pawn, and White can use the move to develop with threats, for instance by pinning the new knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Bxc3+.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight at once, but White recaptures with the knight, so there are no doubled pawns to aim at. Black has handed over the good bishop for no lasting gain, and White regains the e4 pawn with the bishop pair and free development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once, and the answer shapes the whole line. If Black takes on c3, the knight recaptures and White plays on for development and the bishop pair; if the bishop retreats, White simply wins the pawn back.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.N.strategy: Adds a second attacker to e4, but the knight on c3 is pinned, so Black can trade on c3 and hold the pawn with ...Nf6. White is left with doubled pawns and no pawn to show for them.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.B.strategy: Unpins the knight by putting the bishop behind it, so Nxe4 is threatened, and an exchange on c3 can be met by Bxc3 without conceding the pair. But one attacker is easily parried: Black defends with ...Nf6 and White has to find another way to justify the pawn it gave.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Takes the knight and keeps the extra pawn. Black gives up the dark-squared bishop and hands White the bishop pair and a lead in development, which is all the compensation White has; whether it is enough is the question of the whole line.

Retreats and gives the pawn back: White recaptures on e4 at once, so Black avoids the gambit's dangers and keeps both bishops. The game is level, with a sound, undoubled structure for Black and a slight lead in development for White.

Keeps the bishop and the pin for a moment, but 6.b4 drives it to b6 and the knight then takes back the pawn on e4. Black ends with level material and a bishop that presses on a pawn White can easily defend, while White gains queenside space.

Regains the pawn at once, putting a knight on a strong central square. Material is level and White is a little ahead in development, so the gambit has bought time at no cost, though Black's position is sound and safe.

Adds a second attacker to e4 and develops a piece. Black can keep the pawn with ...f5, at the price of a loosened king's side; against ...Nf6 White regains it by exchanging on e4, as it could have done at once. A route back to level material that gains nothing.
Develops the bishop and leaves the e4 pawn for later. It is sound, but quiet: Black simply protects the pawn, and a gambit with no threat behind it has little to show for the pawn.

Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the one on e4, which no piece defends, so White has to deal with it at once. Black gets a normal French set-up, with the bishop on e7 ready for castling and a comfortable game.

Prepares ...Ngf6 so that the knight on d7 can recapture after a trade on f6, which keeps Black's pawn structure intact. It takes an extra move to challenge the knight on e4, but the set-up is solid and the c-pawn stays free for the usual ...c5 break.

Develops with pressure on d4, which stays protected by the knight on e2 and the queen. But the knight sits on the c-pawn's path, so the usual ...c5 break is no longer possible and Black has little with which to challenge White's centre.

Recaptures with the knight from e2, which is the point of 4.Ne2: White keeps its pawn structure intact. In return for the pawn it has the bishop pair and a lead in development, and it is Black who must now defend.

Recaptures with the pawn, which gives up what 4.Ne2 was played for: White's c-pawns are doubled and Black keeps the extra pawn. The bishop pair and open lines are a thin return for a permanently damaged structure.
Interposes instead of recapturing, but Black takes the bishop with check, Bxd2+, and after White retakes it is a whole piece down on top of the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine Gambit, Kan Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Keeps the extra pawn and hits d4, which is attacked twice and defended once. Black develops with a threat, but is still a pawn up with an unfinished kingside and has to find a way to complete development against White's bishops and open lines.

Defends the extra pawn directly and prepares to castle. It is solid but passive: it puts no pressure on White's centre, so White has time to bring the bishop pair and the open lines to bear as compensation for the pawn.
Grabs a second pawn and loses the queen: d4 is guarded by White's queen, which captures first, and Black has nothing to retake with.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.Bg.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Wolf Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Pins the knight on f6 to the queen and threatens to push e5, offering the e4 pawn for speed. Black can take it: after ...dxe4 the knight on c3 is pinned against the king and cannot retake, so White must prove that the lead in development pays.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.e5.strategy: The principled reply: the pawn gains space, drives the knight from f6 and builds a chain from d4 to e5 that cramps Black's kingside. Because the knight on e2 can retake on c3, a trade on c3 no longer doubles White's pawns, so Black has to undermine the chain with ...c5.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.ex.strategy: Trades the central pawns and heads for a symmetrical structure. It is safe, but it gives up White's chance of a space advantage and offers Black easy equality, with the pin on c3 still to be dealt with.
